newsitem.title: USA: Chicago official outlines bond sale plans.
newsitem.headline: Chicago official outlines bond sale plans.

text.p: Chicago's chief financial officer on Thursday outlined the city's near-term plans for bond sales, which include selling water and sewer debt as well as bonds that will help revitalize areas of the city.

Walter Knorr, who accompanied Chicago Mayor Richard Daley to a luncheon sponsored by the Municipal Forum of New York, told Reuters he expected the city to sell about $175 million of water bonds through a syndicate led by Morgan Stanley & Co, and around $75 million of sewer bonds, with Merrill Lynch & Co. serving as lead underwriter.
"These will be done this summer, we're probably talking about August," he said.

Additionally, the tax increment financing program, which helps pay for improvements in various areas of the city to attract new businesses and residents, likely will expand, with around $125 million of bonds expected to be sold in September for the Central Loop.

Approximately $60 million of bonds were planned in 1998 for the Cabrini Green public housing project, but the size of an offering expected for the River South area, as well as its timing, has not yet been set, Knorr said.
The city also was evaluating selling around $25 million of Certificates of Participation to help pay for a new building for municipal employees.

The debt would be repaid through the savings the city would reap by moving the workforce out of the present building, which has very high costs, he explained. The potential savings exceeds the debt service costs.

As part of its budget, Chicago plans to sell in 1998 around $200 million of debt, though Knorr said the city had yet to decide whether this debt would be general obligation or sales tax bonds. Chicago's new budget is not due until autumn.

Asked about additional plans for debt sales, Knorr pointed out that the city's plans for local airports had not been fully fixed. Chicago last year sold about $250 million of revenue bonds as part of an approximately $700 million capital program for Midway.
"We probably don't anticipate doing the next tranche until 1998," he said. However, he added there was a possibility of a refunding for O'Hare, though he noted this hinged on interest rates.
